claims.text: The nanoparticles have an equiatomic Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu composition of 20 at.% each.
The initial nanoparticles are spherical, solid, and based on a random FCC lattice.
The initial FCC lattice parameter is 3.52 Å.
The simulated particle radii span approximately 5–40 Å.
The simulations use classical molecular dynamics with an embedded-atom-method potential.
The particles are heated from 300 to 2500 K in 20 K increments, with 200 ps spent at each temperature.
Element-specific local energy variations predominantly govern melting in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles.
Fe atoms have local potential energies elevated by about 0.5 eV.
Cu's lower elemental melting point contributes to its preferential early mobility.
Fe and Cu become mobile earlier than the other constituent elements.
Preferential early mobility begins in the outer two to three atomic layers and subsequently extends into the core.
Enhanced element-specific diffusion drives coexistence of solid and incipient-liquid regions during melting.
Melting proceeds by a two-phase solid/liquid transition rather than by formation of a persistent unbound surface-liquid shell.
The nanoparticle melting temperature scales inversely with particle radius.
The melting temperature approaches a bulk limit of approximately 2184 K as radius increases.
Early Fe and Cu mobility occurs without significant elemental clustering.
Conventional surface-melting models predict a liquid shell at the nanoparticle surface.
The proposed behavior holds over radii of about 5–40 Å under the specified protocol and interatomic potential.
Particles with radii below approximately 7.5 Å may deviate from the proposed behavior.
Observation of persistent surface-liquid-shell formation, failure of inverse-radius scaling, or absence of early Fe and Cu mobility would refute the hypothesis.
